api/Invex.Process.IProcessRunner.html.title: Interface IProcessRunner | Invex.Process
api/Invex.Process.IProcessRunner.html.summary: Interface IProcessRunner Namespace Invex.Process Assembly Invex.Process.dll Defines a service for executing external processes with comprehensive logging, output capture, and error handling. public interface IProcessRunner Examples Running a tool and inspecting its captured output: var result = await processRunner.RunAsync( new ProcessRunOptions("git", "rev-parse HEAD") { WorkingDirectory = repoRoot, }, cancellationToken); var commitSha = result.Output.Trim(); Remarks Both stdout and stderr are captured in real time via async read loops so that long-running processes stream their output to the logger rather than buffering it until exit. This interface is registered as a singleton by ProcessHostExtensions. Inject it into build targets and helpers instead of using System.Diagnostics.Process directly, to benefit from consistent logging and uniform error handling across all process invocations. Methods Run(ProcessRunOptions) Executes an external process synchronously, blocking until it exits, and returns its result. ProcessRunResult Run(ProcessRunOptions options) Parameters options ProcessRunOptions The configuration for the process execution. Returns ProcessRunResult A ProcessRunResult containing the exit code and captured output. Only returned when the exit code is zero, or when AllowFailedResult is true. Exceptions ProcessException Thrown when the process exits with a non-zero code and AllowFailedResult is false. The message includes the command line, exit code, working directory (when set), and any captured stderr; Result carries the full captured result. Win32Exception Thrown when the executable named by Name cannot be found or started. RunAsync(ProcessRunOptions, CancellationToken) Executes an external process asynchronously and returns its result when it exits. Task<ProcessRunResult> RunAsync(ProcessRunOptions options, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default) Parameters options ProcessRunOptions The configuration for the process execution. cancellationToken CancellationToken A token that cancels the wait for the process to exit. Note: cancelling the token aborts the wait but does not kill the underlying OS process, which continues to run; any output captured so far is discarded. Returns Task<ProcessRunResult> A task that resolves to a ProcessRunResult when the process exits. Only completes successfully when the exit code is zero, or when AllowFailedResult is true. Exceptions ProcessException Thrown (on the returned task) when the process exits with a non-zero code and AllowFailedResult is false. The message includes the command line, exit code, working directory (when set), and any captured stderr; Result carries the full captured result. Win32Exception Thrown when the executable named by Name cannot be found or started. OperationCanceledException Thrown (on the returned task) when cancellationToken is cancelled before the process exits.

api/Invex.Process.ProcessException.html.title: Class ProcessException | Invex.Process
api/Invex.Process.ProcessException.html.summary: Class ProcessException Namespace Invex.Process Assembly Invex.Process.dll The exception thrown by IProcessRunner when a process exits with a non-zero exit code and AllowFailedResult is false. public sealed class ProcessException : Exception Inheritance object Exception ProcessException Examples Inspecting a failed run: try { processRunner.Run(new ProcessRunOptions("git", "rev-parse HEAD")); } catch (ProcessException ex) when (ex.ExitCode == 128) { logger.LogWarning("Not a git repository: {Error}", ex.Result.Error); } Remarks The System.Exception.Message describes the failure (command line, exit code, working directory when set, and any captured stderr), and Result exposes the full result of the failed run — including the captured stdout and stderr and the originating ProcessRunOptions — for programmatic inspection. Derives directly from System.Exception, so existing catch (Exception) blocks continue to handle it. Constructors ProcessException(string, ProcessRunResult) Initializes a new instance of ProcessException for a failed process run. public ProcessException(string message, ProcessRunResult result) Parameters message string The message that describes the failure. result ProcessRunResult The result of the failed process run. Properties ExitCode Gets the non-zero exit code the process returned. public int ExitCode { get; } Property Value int Remarks Shorthand for Result.ExitCode. Result Gets the result of the failed process run, including the captured stdout and stderr and the options the process was run with. public ProcessRunResult Result { get; } Property Value ProcessRunResult

api/Invex.Process.ProcessHostExtensions..summary: Class ProcessHostExtensions Namespace Invex.Process Assembly Invex.Process.dll Provides extension methods for registering the process runner service with an Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection.IServiceCollection. public static class ProcessHostExtensions Inheritance object ProcessHostExtensions Methods AddProcessRunner(IServiceCollection) Registers IProcessRunner as a singleton backed by the default Invex.Process.ProcessRunner implementation. public static IServiceCollection AddProcessRunner(this IServiceCollection serviceCollection) Parameters serviceCollection IServiceCollection Returns IServiceCollection The same Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection.IServiceCollection for further configuration. api/Invex.Process.ProcessRunOptions.html.title: Class ProcessRunOptions | Invex.Process
api/Invex.Process.ProcessRunOptions.html.summary: Class ProcessRunOptions Namespace Invex.Process Assembly Invex.Process.dll Immutable configuration for a single external-process execution through IProcessRunner. public sealed record ProcessRunOptions Inheritance object ProcessRunOptions Examples Running a quiet, failure-tolerant invocation with a custom environment: var options = new ProcessRunOptions("dotnet", ["build", "--configuration", configuration]) { WorkingDirectory = projectDirectory, InvocationLogLevel = LogLevel.Debug, AllowFailedResult = true, EnvironmentVariables = { ["DOTNET_NOLOGO"] = "1" }, }; Remarks All properties have defaults suited to typical build-automation use: invocation is logged at Microsoft.Extensions.Logging.LogLevel.Information, stdout at Microsoft.Extensions.Logging.LogLevel.Debug, and stderr at Microsoft.Extensions.Logging.LogLevel.Warning. A non-zero exit code throws a ProcessException by default so build steps fail fast without requiring callers to check exit codes manually. Both stdout and stderr are fully captured into ProcessRunResult regardless of log level, so callers can inspect the full output even when logs are suppressed. Constructors ProcessRunOptions(string, string) Immutable configuration for a single external-process execution through IProcessRunner. public ProcessRunOptions(string Name, string Args) Parameters Name string The name or path of the executable to run (e.g. "dotnet", "git"). Args string The command-line arguments to pass to the executable as a pre-joined string. Examples Running a quiet, failure-tolerant invocation with a custom environment: var options = new ProcessRunOptions("dotnet", ["build", "--configuration", configuration]) { WorkingDirectory = projectDirectory, InvocationLogLevel = LogLevel.Debug, AllowFailedResult = true, EnvironmentVariables = { ["DOTNET_NOLOGO"] = "1" }, }; Remarks All properties have defaults suited to typical build-automation use: invocation is logged at Microsoft.Extensions.Logging.LogLevel.Information, stdout at Microsoft.Extensions.Logging.LogLevel.Debug, and stderr at Microsoft.Extensions.Logging.LogLevel.Warning. A non-zero exit code throws a ProcessException by default so build steps fail fast without requiring callers to check exit codes manually. Both stdout and stderr are fully captured into ProcessRunResult regardless of log level, so callers can inspect the full output even when logs are suppressed. ProcessRunOptions(string, string[]) Initializes a new instance of ProcessRunOptions from an array of argument tokens, joining them with a single space. public ProcessRunOptions(string Name, string[] Args) Parameters Name string The name or path of the executable to run. Args string[] An array of argument tokens. Empty and whitespace-only entries are removed before joining so that optional arguments can be passed as string.Empty without creating spurious spaces in the final argument string. Properties AllowFailedResult Gets a value indicating whether a non-zero exit code should be tolerated rather than throwing an exception. public bool AllowFailedResult { get; init; } Property Value bool Remarks When false (the default), Run(ProcessRunOptions) and RunAsync(ProcessRunOptions, CancellationToken) throw if the exit code is non-zero, which causes the enclosing build target to fail immediately. Set to true when the caller needs to inspect the result regardless of success — for example, running a linter and deciding separately whether to fail the build. The caller must then check ExitCode explicitly. Args The command-line arguments to pass to the executable as a pre-joined string. public string Args { get; init; } Property Value string EnvironmentVariables Gets the environment variables to inject into the process's environment. public Dictionary<string, string?> EnvironmentVariables { get; init; } Property Value Dictionary<string, string> Remarks Keys are variable names and values are their string values. A null value removes the inherited variable from the child process's environment. Variables not listed here are inherited from the current process unchanged. Only the variable names appear in the invocation log line (see InvocationLogLevel); their values are never logged. ErrorLogLevel Gets the log level used when streaming each line of the process's standard error. public LogLevel ErrorLogLevel { get; init; } Property Value LogLevel Remarks Defaults to Microsoft.Extensions.Logging.LogLevel.Warning. Like OutputLogLevel, the full stderr is captured into Error irrespective of this value. On a non-zero exit, when this level is below Microsoft.Extensions.Logging.LogLevel.Information, the complete captured stderr is additionally re-logged at Microsoft.Extensions.Logging.LogLevel.Warning so failure diagnostics remain visible. InvocationLogLevel Gets the log level used when logging the process invocation line (e.g. Run: dotnet build --configuration Release). public LogLevel InvocationLogLevel { get; init; } Property Value LogLevel Remarks Defaults to Microsoft.Extensions.Logging.LogLevel.Information. Lower this to Microsoft.Extensions.Logging.LogLevel.Debug for noisy or frequently-called sub-processes. The invocation line includes the full Args, the WorkingDirectory when set, and the names of any EnvironmentVariables. Environment variable values are never logged, so they are a safer way to pass secrets than command-line arguments. When a secret must be passed as an argument, lower this level (or set it to Microsoft.Extensions.Logging.LogLevel.None) to keep it out of the log. Name The name or path of the executable to run (e.g. "dotnet", "git"). public string Name { get; init; } Property Value string OutputLogLevel Gets the log level used when streaming each line of the process's standard output. public LogLevel OutputLogLevel { get; init; } Property Value LogLevel Remarks Defaults to Microsoft.Extensions.Logging.LogLevel.Debug. The full stdout is still captured into Output regardless of this setting, so callers can inspect it even when debug logging is disabled. Set to Microsoft.Extensions.Logging.LogLevel.None to suppress stdout entirely from the log. On a non-zero exit, when this level is below Microsoft.Extensions.Logging.LogLevel.Information, the complete captured stdout is additionally re-logged at Microsoft.Extensions.Logging.LogLevel.Information so failure diagnostics remain visible. TransformError Gets an optional per-line transformation applied to each line of the process's standard error before it is logged and captured. public Func<string, string?>? TransformError { get; init; } Property Value Func<string, string> Remarks Behaves identically to TransformOutput but operates on stderr. Returning null suppresses the line from both the log and Error. TransformOutput Gets an optional per-line transformation applied to each line of the process's standard output before it is logged and captured. public Func<string, string?>? TransformOutput { get; init; } Property Value Func<string, string> Remarks The delegate receives a raw non-null line (null data events are filtered before the delegate is called). Returning null suppresses the line entirely — it is neither logged nor included in Output. This is useful for filtering noisy progress lines or redacting secrets from captured output. WorkingDirectory Gets the working directory for the process execution. public string? WorkingDirectory { get; init; } Property Value string Remarks When null (the default), the process inherits the current application's working directory. Set this when a tool must be run from a specific project or repository root.

api/Invex.Process.ProcessRunResult.html.title: Class ProcessRunResult | Invex.Process
api/Invex.Process.ProcessRunResult.html.summary: Class ProcessRunResult Namespace Invex.Process Assembly Invex.Process.dll Represents the result of a completed external-process execution. public sealed record ProcessRunResult Inheritance object ProcessRunResult Remarks Both Output and Error are always populated with whatever the process wrote, regardless of the log levels configured in RunOptions. This means callers can inspect the full output in error-handling logic even when debug logging was disabled during the run. Lines suppressed by TransformOutput or TransformError (i.e. where the transform returned null) are excluded from the captured text; transformed lines appear in their transformed form. For processes run with AllowFailedResult set to false (the default), this record is only returned when ExitCode is zero — otherwise IProcessRunner throws before returning. ExitCode int The exit code returned by the process upon termination. Output string The complete standard output (stdout) captured from the process. docs/cancellation.html.title: Cancellation | Invex.Process
docs/cancellation.html.summary: Cancellation Read this page before putting a timeout on a process run: RunAsync accepts a CancellationToken, but it cancels the wait for the process to exit, not the process itself. For example, to stop waiting after five minutes: using var cts = new CancellationTokenSource(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(5)); try { var result = await processRunner.RunAsync( new ProcessRunOptions("dotnet", "test"), cts.Token); } catch (OperationCanceledException) { // The wait was abandoned after 5 minutes. } What cancellation does — and doesn't — do Important Cancelling the token aborts the wait, not the process. The underlying OS process keeps running after OperationCanceledException is thrown. When the token fires: The returned task faults with OperationCanceledException (a TaskCanceledException). Output captured up to that point is discarded — you do not receive a partial ProcessRunResult. The child process continues running to completion (or until it is killed externally). This design keeps the runner predictable: it never kills processes it didn't decide to start killing, which matters for tools that hold locks or write files non-atomically. Killing the process yourself If you need hard timeout semantics — "stop waiting and terminate the tool" — run the process through a wrapper that owns process-tree termination, or kill by name/ID after cancellation: try { await processRunner.RunAsync(options, cts.Token); } catch (OperationCanceledException) { foreach (var p in System.Diagnostics.Process.GetProcessesByName("stuck-tool")) p.Kill(entireProcessTree: true); throw; } Synchronous Run The synchronous Run method has no cancellation support — it blocks until the process exits. Prefer RunAsync whenever a timeout or cooperative cancellation may be needed. See also Running Processes: sync versus async execution. Handling Failures: the other ways a run can end without a result. IProcessRunner

docs/getting-started.html.title: Getting Started | Invex.Process
docs/getting-started.html.summary: Getting Started This page takes you from installing the package to running your first process and reading its result. Start here if you are adding Invex.Process to a host, tool or build for the first time. Installation dotnet add package Invex.Process The package targets net10.0. Register the service Add the process runner to your dependency injection container once during host setup: using Invex.Process; using Microsoft.Extensions.Hosting; var builder = Host.CreateApplicationBuilder(args); builder.Services.AddProcessRunner(); AddProcessRunner() registers IProcessRunner as a singleton. The runner is stateless, so a single instance can safely serve concurrent callers. Note The runner logs through ILogger<ProcessRunner>, so make sure logging is configured on the host (it is by default with Host.CreateApplicationBuilder). Run your first process Inject IProcessRunner and call RunAsync (or the synchronous Run): using Invex.Process; public sealed class VersionReporter(IProcessRunner processRunner) { public async Task<string> GetDotnetVersionAsync(CancellationToken cancellationToken) { var result = await processRunner.RunAsync( new ProcessRunOptions("dotnet", "--version"), cancellationToken); return result.Output.Trim(); } } When this runs you'll see log entries like: info: Invex.Process.ProcessRunner[0] Run: dotnet --version dbug: Invex.Process.ProcessRunner[0] 10.0.100 What you get back Both Run and RunAsync return a ProcessRunResult: Property Description ExitCode The process exit code. Zero unless AllowFailedResult was set (a non-zero code otherwise throws). Output The complete captured stdout, one line per Environment.NewLine. Error The complete captured stderr. RunOptions The options the process was started with. The output is always fully captured — even if you turn logging down or off entirely. Next steps Running Processes: arguments, working directories, environment variables. Handling Failures: what happens when the exit code isn't zero. Logging: tune how invocations and output are logged. IProcessRunner, ProcessRunOptions and ProcessRunResult in the API reference.

docs/handling-failures.html.title: Handling Failures | Invex.Process
docs/handling-failures.html.summary: Handling Failures This page explains what happens when a process exits with a non-zero code or cannot be started at all, and how to opt out of the default exception when a failure is an expected outcome. Fail-fast by default When a process exits with a non-zero exit code, Run and RunAsync throw a ProcessException rather than returning a result. This means build steps and tools fail immediately without callers having to remember to check exit codes: // Throws if the build fails. processRunner.Run(new ProcessRunOptions("dotnet", "build --configuration Release")); The exception message is designed to be actionable on its own: Process 'dotnet' failed with exit code 1 Command: dotnet build --configuration Release Working Directory: /repo/src Error Output: MSBUILD : error MSB1009: Project file does not exist. It includes: the executable name and exit code, the full command line, the working directory (when one was set), the captured stderr (when the process wrote any). ProcessException derives from Exception and also exposes the failure programmatically: ExitCode and Result (the full ProcessRunResult, with captured stdout/stderr and the original ProcessRunOptions): try { processRunner.Run(new ProcessRunOptions("git", "rev-parse HEAD")); } catch (ProcessException ex) when (ex.ExitCode == 128) { Console.WriteLine($"Not a git repository: {ex.Result.Error}"); } Tolerating failures with AllowFailedResult Sometimes a non-zero exit code is an expected outcome you want to inspect — linters, format verifiers, git diff --exit-code, and similar. Set AllowFailedResult to receive the result instead of an exception: var result = processRunner.Run(new ProcessRunOptions("dotnet", "format --verify-no-changes") { AllowFailedResult = true, }); if (result.ExitCode != 0) { Console.WriteLine("Formatting issues found:"); Console.WriteLine(result.Output); } Warning With AllowFailedResult = true it becomes your responsibility to check result.ExitCode. Forgetting the check silently swallows failures. Failure visibility in logs On any non-zero exit — whether or not AllowFailedResult is set — the runner makes sure the failure is visible in the logs even if per-line output logging was quiet: If OutputLogLevel was below Information, the full captured stdout is re-logged at Information. If ErrorLogLevel was below Information, the full captured stderr is re-logged at Warning. So a process that ran with OutputLogLevel = LogLevel.Debug (the default) still shows its complete output in the logs when it fails, without you having to re-run at a higher verbosity. Startup failures If the executable itself cannot be found or started (bad name, not on PATH, missing file), the underlying Process.Start call throws System.ComponentModel.Win32Exception. This is distinct from a process that starts and then exits non-zero. try { processRunner.Run(new ProcessRunOptions("definitely-not-a-real-tool", "")); } catch (Win32Exception ex) { // Tool not installed / not on PATH } See also Logging: failure promotion in detail. Testing Your Code: simulating failures in unit tests. IProcessRunner, ProcessRunOptions, ProcessRunResult and ProcessException

docs/introduction.html.title: Introduction | Invex.Process
docs/introduction.html.summary: Introduction Invex.Process runs external executables from .NET code through one injectable service. This page explains the problem it solves, when it is (and is not) the right tool, and the principles behind its behavior. The problem Shelling out to external tools (dotnet, git, npm, docker, …) from .NET code with the raw System.Diagnostics.Process API requires a surprising amount of boilerplate to get right: Redirecting stdout and stderr and wiring up asynchronous read loops so long-running processes don't deadlock on full pipe buffers. Accumulating output for later inspection while also surfacing it live in logs. Checking exit codes and producing useful error messages when something fails. Plumbing in working directories and environment variables. Doing all of the above consistently across every call site. Most codebases end up with a half-dozen subtly different copies of this logic. The solution Invex.Process wraps all of this behind a single injectable abstraction: var result = await processRunner.RunAsync( new ProcessRunOptions("git", "rev-parse HEAD"), cancellationToken); var commitSha = result.Output.Trim(); One line of registration (services.AddProcessRunner()), one options record describing what to run, one result record telling you what happened — and consistent logging and error handling everywhere. When to use it Invex.Process fits well when: Build targets, CLI tools or services shell out to command-line tools and you want every call logged and checked the same way. You want a non-zero exit code to fail the operation by default, with an actionable message. You want to unit-test code that runs processes without starting real ones. It is probably not the right tool when: You need to write to the process's standard input or interact with it while it runs. Only stdout and stderr are redirected. You need hard timeouts that kill the process. Cancellation stops the wait, not the process (see Cancellation). You need binary output or a raw stream. Output is read and captured line by line as text. You need shell features such as pipes, globbing or redirection. The executable is started directly with a single argument string; run a shell explicitly if you need one. Design principles Fail fast by default. A non-zero exit code throws a descriptive ProcessException that includes the command line, exit code, working directory, and captured stderr. Opt out per-invocation with AllowFailedResult when you want to handle failures yourself. Never lose output. Full stdout and stderr are always captured into the result, regardless of how (or whether) they were logged. Stream, don't buffer. Output is logged line-by-line in real time, so long-running processes show progress as they go. Stay testable. Your code depends on the IProcessRunner interface, which is trivial to fake in unit tests — no real processes needed. Key concepts at a glance The entire public surface is four types in one namespace (Invex.Process): Type Role IProcessRunner The service you inject: Run(options) / RunAsync(options, ct). ProcessRunOptions Immutable record describing one invocation. ProcessRunResult Immutable record describing the outcome. ProcessHostExtensions AddProcessRunner() DI registration. Next steps Getting Started: install the package and run your first process. Running Processes: arguments, working directories and environment variables. API Reference: the four public types.

docs/logging.html.title: Logging | Invex.Process
docs/logging.html.summary: Logging The runner logs through the standard Microsoft.Extensions.Logging abstractions (ILogger<ProcessRunner>), so output flows to whatever providers your host configures — console, Application Insights, Serilog, etc. What gets logged Each invocation produces three kinds of log entries: The invocation line — logged once when the process starts: Run: dotnet build --configuration Release in /repo/src with env CI, NUGET_API_KEY The working directory and environment variables are included only when set. Only the environment variable names are logged, never their values. Output lines — each stdout line, streamed in real time as the process runs. Error lines — each stderr line, streamed in real time. Tuning log levels All three are configurable per invocation via ProcessRunOptions: Property Default Controls InvocationLogLevel Information The Run: … line. OutputLogLevel Debug Each stdout line. ErrorLogLevel Warning Each stderr line. var options = new ProcessRunOptions("dotnet", "test") { InvocationLogLevel = LogLevel.Debug, // quieter invocation line OutputLogLevel = LogLevel.Information, // show test output at info ErrorLogLevel = LogLevel.Error, // treat stderr lines as errors }; Use LogLevel.None to suppress a stream from the log entirely. Note Log levels only affect logging. The full stdout and stderr are always captured into ProcessRunResult.Output / ProcessRunResult.Error regardless of these settings. Failure promotion When a process exits non-zero, quiet output is automatically promoted so the failure is diagnosable from the logs: stdout configured below Information → re-logged in full at Information; stderr configured below Information → re-logged in full at Warning. This happens before the exception is thrown (and also when AllowFailedResult tolerates the failure). The common pattern is therefore: Leave OutputLogLevel at Debug so successful runs are quiet. Rely on promotion to surface the full output automatically when something fails. Secrets in logs Two things to watch: The invocation line includes the full command arguments and the names (not values) of any environment variables you set. Prefer passing secrets through EnvironmentVariables; if a secret must go on the command line, lower InvocationLogLevel (or set it to LogLevel.None). The exception thrown on a non-zero exit also includes the full command line. Output lines may echo secrets printed by the tool. Use TransformOutput / TransformError to redact or suppress them — see Transforming Output. See also Transforming Output: redacting and filtering lines before they are logged. Handling Failures: what happens after a non-zero exit is logged. ProcessRunOptions

docs/running-processes.html.title: Running Processes | Invex.Process
docs/running-processes.html.summary: Running Processes Every invocation is described by a single immutable ProcessRunOptions record. This page covers the core execution options; failure handling and logging have their own pages. Sync or async IProcessRunner exposes two methods: // Blocks the calling thread until the process exits. ProcessRunResult Run(ProcessRunOptions options); // Awaits process exit; supports cancellation. Task<ProcessRunResult> RunAsync(ProcessRunOptions options, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default); Both behave identically apart from threading: same logging, same capture, same failure handling. Prefer RunAsync in async code paths and anywhere you want cancellation support (see Cancellation). Passing arguments Arguments can be supplied as a single pre-joined string or as an array of tokens: // As a single string var options = new ProcessRunOptions("git", "status --short"); // As tokens var options2 = new ProcessRunOptions("git", ["status", "--short"]); When using the array form, empty and whitespace-only entries are removed before joining. This makes conditional arguments clean — no spurious double spaces: var verbose = ShouldBeVerbose(); var options = new ProcessRunOptions("git", [ "status", "--short", verbose ? "--verbose" : "", // dropped entirely when empty ]); Important Arguments are ultimately passed to the OS as a single string (ProcessStartInfo.Arguments). If an argument value can contain spaces or special characters (e.g. a user-supplied file path), quote it yourself: $"\"{path}\"". Working directory By default the child process inherits the current process's working directory. Set WorkingDirectory to run a tool from a specific location: var result = processRunner.Run(new ProcessRunOptions("npm", "ci") { WorkingDirectory = "/repo/frontend", }); Environment variables EnvironmentVariables lets you add, override, or remove variables for the child process. Variables you don't list are inherited unchanged from the current process: var result = processRunner.Run(new ProcessRunOptions("npm", "ci") { EnvironmentVariables = { ["NODE_ENV"] = "production", // add or override ["CI"] = "true", ["NPM_TOKEN"] = null, // a null value removes the inherited variable }, }); The invocation log line includes the variables you set, so be careful not to put secrets in values you don't want logged (or lower InvocationLogLevel — see Logging). Reusing and varying options ProcessRunOptions is a record, so you can keep a baseline and vary it with with: var git = new ProcessRunOptions("git", "") { WorkingDirectory = repoRoot, InvocationLogLevel = LogLevel.Debug, }; var status = git with { Args = "status --short" }; var fetch = git with { Args = "fetch --prune" }; Concurrency IProcessRunner is stateless and registered as a singleton — it is safe to run multiple processes concurrently from multiple threads. See also Handling Failures: non-zero exit codes and startup failures. Logging: what the invocation line contains. Cancellation: cancelling RunAsync. IProcessRunner and ProcessRunOptions

docs/testing.html.title: Testing Your Code | Invex.Process
docs/testing.html.summary: Testing Your Code Because your code depends on the IProcessRunner interface, unit tests never have to start real processes. Fake the interface, return canned ProcessRunResult instances, and assert on the options your code passed in. The examples below use FakeItEasy, but any mocking library (or a hand-rolled fake) works the same way. Returning a canned result [Test] public async Task GetDotnetVersion_returns_trimmed_output() { var processRunner = A.Fake<IProcessRunner>(); A.CallTo(() => processRunner.RunAsync(A<ProcessRunOptions>._, A<CancellationToken>._)) .ReturnsLazily((ProcessRunOptions options, CancellationToken _) => new ProcessRunResult(options, 0, "10.0.100\n", "")); var reporter = new VersionReporter(processRunner); var version = await reporter.GetDotnetVersionAsync(CancellationToken.None); Assert.That(version, Is.EqualTo("10.0.100")); } Asserting on the invocation ProcessRunOptions is a record, so captured options are easy to inspect: [Test] public async Task Build_runs_dotnet_in_the_project_directory() { var processRunner = A.Fake<IProcessRunner>(); ProcessRunOptions? captured = null; A.CallTo(() => processRunner.RunAsync(A<ProcessRunOptions>._, A<CancellationToken>._)) .Invokes((ProcessRunOptions options, CancellationToken _) => captured = options) .ReturnsLazily((ProcessRunOptions options, CancellationToken _) => new ProcessRunResult(options, 0, "", "")); await new Builder(processRunner).BuildAsync("/repo/src/App", CancellationToken.None); Assert.That(captured!.Name, Is.EqualTo("dotnet")); Assert.That(captured.Args, Does.Contain("build")); Assert.That(captured.WorkingDirectory, Is.EqualTo("/repo/src/App")); } Simulating failure To test failure-handling paths, either return a non-zero result (for code using AllowFailedResult) or have the fake throw (mirroring the default fail-fast behavior): // Code under test sets AllowFailedResult and inspects ExitCode: A.CallTo(() => processRunner.RunAsync(A<ProcessRunOptions>._, A<CancellationToken>._)) .ReturnsLazily((ProcessRunOptions options, CancellationToken _) => new ProcessRunResult(options, 1, "", "fatal: not a git repository")); // Code under test relies on the default throwing behavior: A.CallTo(() => processRunner.RunAsync(A<ProcessRunOptions>._, A<CancellationToken>._)) .Throws((ProcessRunOptions options, CancellationToken _) => new ProcessException( "Process 'git' failed with exit code 128", new ProcessRunResult(options, 128, "", "fatal: not a git repository"))); Tips Don't fake what you don't own in integration tests. For end-to-end confidence, run a real, harmless executable (e.g. dotnet --version) against the real runner registered via AddProcessRunner(). Keep options construction in testable seams. If a class builds complex ProcessRunOptions, consider exposing that construction through an internal method you can assert on directly. Remember the contract: with default options, your code only ever sees results with ExitCode == 0; non-zero exits arrive as exceptions. See also Handling Failures: the exception your fakes should mirror. Getting Started: the VersionReporter example used above. IProcessRunner, ProcessRunOptions and ProcessRunResult

docs/transforming-output.html.title: Transforming Output | Invex.Process
docs/transforming-output.html.summary: Transforming Output ProcessRunOptions.TransformOutput and ProcessRunOptions.TransformError are optional per-line hooks applied to stdout and stderr respectively, before each line is logged and captured. Each delegate has the shape Func<string, string?>: It receives the raw line (never null — null data events are filtered out beforehand). Return the same string to pass the line through unchanged. Return a different string to rewrite the line. Return null to suppress the line entirely — it is neither logged nor included in ProcessRunResult.Output / ProcessRunResult.Error. Redacting secrets var options = new ProcessRunOptions("deploy", "--token " + token) { TransformOutput = line => line.Contains(token) ? line.Replace(token, "[redacted]") : line, }; The redaction applies to both the live log stream and the captured result.Output. Warning Transforms only see the process's output lines. The invocation line (Run: deploy --token …) is logged before the process starts and includes the full arguments (environment variables are logged by name only), so a secret passed on the command line still reaches the log at InvocationLogLevel. See Logging. Filtering noise Drop high-volume progress lines that would otherwise flood the logs and the captured output: var options = new ProcessRunOptions("docker", "build .") { TransformError = line => line.StartsWith("#") || line.Contains("DONE") ? null // suppressed: not logged, not captured : line, }; Normalizing output Transforms can also reshape lines for downstream parsing: var options = new ProcessRunOptions("git", "status --porcelain") { TransformOutput = line => line.TrimEnd(), }; Behavioral notes Transforms run on the process's output-reader callbacks, once per line, as lines arrive. Keep them fast and side-effect-free. A suppressed line is excluded from failure promotion too — if the process fails, the re-logged "full output" is the captured (post-transform) output. Transforms are per-invocation. For a shared policy, build a helper that returns pre-configured ProcessRunOptions instances, or wrap the delegate in a reusable method. See also Logging: log levels and failure promotion. Running Processes: the rest of ProcessRunOptions. ProcessRunOptions and ProcessRunResult

docs/versioning.html.title: Versioning | Invex.Process
docs/versioning.html.summary: Versioning This page describes what a version number change means for you as a consumer of the package, so you know which upgrades are safe to take without code changes. Invex.Process follows Semantic Versioning 2.0.0. Version numbers take the form MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH and are derived automatically from the Git history via GitVersion. What the numbers mean Component Bumped when Examples MAJOR A breaking change is made to the public API. Removing or renaming a public type or member, changing a method signature, changing a default value in a behavior-breaking way, dropping a target framework. MINOR New functionality is added in a backward-compatible way. New optional properties on ProcessRunOptions, new overloads, new extension methods, adding a target framework. PATCH A backward-compatible bug fix or internal improvement is made. Fixing incorrect output capture, logging corrections, documentation, performance improvements. What counts as the public API The public API is everything reachable from a consuming assembly: Public types: IProcessRunner, ProcessRunOptions, ProcessRunResult, ProcessHostExtensions. Their public members, signatures, and parameter names (named arguments are part of the contract). Documented behavioral contracts — for example, "a non-zero exit code throws unless AllowFailedResult is true" and "stdout/stderr are always fully captured into the result". Supported target frameworks. The public API surface is tracked and enforced at build time with public API analyzers, so unintended breaking changes fail the build before they ship. What is not covered internal types (e.g. the ProcessRunner implementation class) — depend on IProcessRunner, not on the concrete type. Exact log message templates and wording — these may be refined in MINOR/PATCH releases. The exact text of exception messages. Pre-release versions Pre-release packages (e.g. 2.1.0-beta.3) may include API changes between pre-release builds without a MAJOR bump. They are intended for early feedback, not production use. See also Introduction: the library's design principles, which are part of its behavioral contract. API Reference: the public types covered by this policy.

index.html.title: Invex.Process | Invex.Process
index.html.summary: Invex.Process A small, focused .NET library for running external processes with first-class logging, real-time output streaming, full output capture, and fail-fast error handling. It wraps System.Diagnostics.Process behind a clean, injectable IProcessRunner abstraction so your build targets, tools, and services can shell out to executables (dotnet, git, npm, …) without re-implementing redirection, buffering, and exit-code handling every time. Start here Introduction: the problem it solves and when to use it. Getting Started: install the package, register it and run your first process. Running Processes: arguments, working directories and environment variables. Handling Failures: fail-fast exceptions and AllowFailedResult. API Reference: every public type.
